subject: Manufacturing
title: How Laptops Get Featherweight Metal Shells

thixotropic_slurry.title: Thixotropic Shear Thinning & Slurry Rheology
thixotropic_slurry.body:
Thixotropy is the time-dependent shear-thinning property of pseudoplastic fluids. In a resting semi-solid state between solidus (470°C) and liquidus (595°C), magnesium forms an interconnected network of solid particles exhibiting high apparent viscosity.

Apparent Viscosity (Power-Law Rheology):
$$\eta = K \cdot \dot{\gamma}^{n - 1} \cdot \exp\left(\frac{B}{T}\right)$$
Flow behavior index $n \approx 0.35$ • Shear rate $\dot{\gamma} > 10^4\text{ s}^{-1}$ inside nozzle • Dynamic viscosity $\eta$ collapses from $\sim 100\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$ to $< 0.1\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$

Under the high-speed rotational shear of the injection screw, mechanical shear stress fractures dendritic crystals into compact, spheroidal globules, causing viscosity to drop by three orders of magnitude and allowing the slurry to flow like a warm liquid into microscopic die ribs.

globular_microstructure.title: Globular α-Mg Rosettes & Solid Fraction
globular_microstructure.body:
Standard high-pressure die casting solidifies from a fully liquid melt, producing coarse dendritic grain structures prone to shrinkage voids and hot tearing. Thixomolding precisely controls the solid fraction ($f_s$) between 5% and 30%.

Scheil-Gulliver Solidification Fraction:
$$f_s = 1 - \left(\frac{T_m - T}{T_m - T_L}\right)^{\frac{1}{1 - k_0}}$$
Target process window: $f_s \approx 0.08 - 0.20$ ($565^\circ\text{C} - 580^\circ\text{C}$) • Spheroidal $\alpha$-Mg rosettes in eutectic $\text{Mg}_{17}\text{Al}_{12}$

The rounded non-dendritic α-magnesium rosettes eliminate internal stress concentrations, reducing volumetric solidification shrinkage from ~4.5% down to <1.5% and virtually eliminating hot-crack propagation during rapid cooling.

dievar_steel.title: Uddeholm Dievar vs. AISI H13 Hot-Work Tool Steel
dievar_steel.body:
Tooling inserts experience extreme cyclic thermal shock, cycling from 200°C mold preheat to 580°C metal contact every 20 seconds. Standard AISI H13 tool steel fails via gross heat checking (network micro-cracks) after 70,000 shots due to silicon segregation.

Thermal Shock Resistance Index:
$$R_{\text{th}} = \frac{k \cdot \sigma_y}{E \cdot \alpha}$$
Uddeholm Dievar (0.2% Si, 2.3% Mo) • Charpy V-Notch Toughness: $> 18\text{ J}$ @ $20^\circ\text{C}$ (vs. H13 $\approx 8 - 10\text{ J}$) • Tool Life: $> 250{,}000$ cycles

Dievar's superior ductile fracture toughness and resistance to temper softening inhibit thermal fatigue micro-crack initiation along sharp cosmetic corner radii and thin shut-off lands.

porosity_entrainment.title: Laminar Frontal Ingress vs. Gas Entrainment Porosity
porosity_entrainment.body:
In conventional die casting, superheated liquid metal enters the die at 40–80 m/s in a highly turbulent spray (Weber number $\text{We} > 100$), entraining mold cavity air, steam, and evaporated lubricants into micro-bubbles that cause internal blistering.

Hydraulic Cavity Filling Regime:
$$\text{Re} = \frac{\rho \cdot v \cdot D_h}{\eta} < 2{,}300 \quad (\text{Stable Laminar Flow})$$
Bingham pseudoplastic flow • Internal gas voids $< 0.2\%$ (vs. $> 3.5\%$ in HPDC) • Enables blister-free T6 heat treating and laser welding

The high resting viscosity of semi-solid slurry maintains a coherent, cohesive frontal flow wave that pushes air cleanly toward perimeter chill vents without trapping pockets of gas in thin-wall sections.

damping_capacity.title: Specific Damping Capacity (SDC) & Acoustic Dissipation
damping_capacity.body:
Magnesium possesses the highest internal friction and specific damping capacity of all engineering metals, making it an exceptional structural damper for handheld and portable electronics.

Specific Damping Capacity (SDC):
$$\text{SDC} = \left(\frac{\Delta W}{W}\right) \times 100\%$$
Cast AZ91D Mg: $42\% - 58\%$ • 6061-T6 Al: $4\% - 8\%$ ($8\times$ lower) • Hexagonal close-packed lattice dislocations convert shock into lattice heat

When an enclosure is dropped or subjected to high-frequency fan vibration, dislocation motion within the hexagonal close-packed (HCP) magnesium lattice dissipates mechanical energy directly into lattice heat, damping shock before it transmits to brittle display glass.

micro_arc_oxidation.title: Micro-Arc Oxidation (MAO / PEO) Ceramic Barrier
micro_arc_oxidation.body:
Magnesium is highly electrochemically active ($E^\circ = -2.37\text{ V}$) and cannot be anodized like aluminum because magnesium hydroxide $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is chemically porous and unstable in acidic or saline conditions.

Plasma Electrolytic Oxidation Breakdown:
$$V_{\text{arc}} \approx 400 - 550\text{ V AC} \quad (100\text{ Hz} - 2\text{ kHz})$$
Synthesizes crystalline $\alpha\text{-Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{MgAl}_2\text{O}_4$ spinel • $> 500\text{ Hours}$ ASTM B117 salt spray with 0 pits • Dielectric breakdown $> 1.5\text{ kV}$

Micro-Arc Oxidation uses high-voltage micro-discharges in an alkaline silicate electrolyte to grow a continuous, ceramic-grade spinel layer metallurgically bonded into the magnesium substrate, providing extreme scratch resistance and corrosion immunity.

ISSUE #003•MANUFACTURING•15 MIN READ

How Laptops Get Featherweight Metal Shells

Why injection molding semi-solid magnesium slurry beats 5-axis CNC machining for sub-millimeter ultrabooks—and how laminar metal flow unlocks featherweight unibody stiffness.

1. The Structural Challenge: Sub-Millimeter Stiffness in Mobile Computing

Ultra-portable hardware—from flagship ultrabooks to VR headset frames—faces an uncompromising mechanical contradiction. Industrial design demands thinner chassis walls (often dropping below 0.60 mm) to conserve internal stack height for high-capacity battery pouches, vapor chambers, and keyboard travel. Simultaneously, reliability engineering imposes strict stiffness floors: an enclosure must resist torsional flex under single-handed palm-rest pick-up, survive 4-foot corner drops without crushing internal logic boards, and feel unyielding in the hand.

For fifteen years, the consumer standard has been the CNC-machined aluminum unibody. Pioneered at volume with the MacBook Air, this architecture mills monolithic top-cases from extruded 6061-T6 aluminum. While billet CNC machining delivers exceptional precision (±0.015 mm tolerances) and premium Type-II anodization, it encounters severe physical and economic limits when nominal walls drop below 0.75 mm.

What is Thixomolding, and Why Does It Beat CNC Machining?
Rather than melting metal into a hazardous liquid pot (like die casting) or carving a solid 1.45 kg aluminum block down to size over 45 minutes of subtractive spindle time, Thixomolding feeds solid magnesium chips into a heated reciprocating screw barrel. The barrel warms the metal into a semi-solid 'slurry'—half-solid, half-liquid, with the consistency of soft-serve ice cream or a Slurpee—and rapidly injects it into a precision steel mold under 120 MPa of hydraulic pressure.

Against 5-axis CNC machining, this delivers four decisive engineering advantages:

  • Blistering Cycle Time (18 Seconds vs. 45 Minutes): A 5-axis CNC setup spends 45 to 55 minutes hogging pockets and profiling ribs out of extruded billet. A thixomolding cell injects the entire net-shape enclosure in an 18-second cycle time, requiring only a quick 90-second secondary CNC cleanup for hinge threads and cosmetic chamfers.
  • Zero Feedstock Waste (>92% vs. <10% Utilization): CNC hogging converts over 90% of an expensive aluminum billet directly into scrap swarf (buy-to-fly ratio exceeding 10:1). Thixomolding injects only the required 165 grams, and the runner system is ground directly back into granules for closed-loop hopper reuse.
  • Sub-Millimeter Thin Walls Without Cutter Deflection: When milling 0.50 mm walls on a CNC router, cutting forces from the endmill cause thin aluminum walls to chatter, vibrate, and deflect away from the tool, ruining tolerances. Thixomolding flows directly into 0.50 mm mold cavities without cutting tool deflection.
  • The Plate Bending Stiffness Equation: The resistance of a flat structural panel to flexural bending is governed by its flexural plate rigidity $D$:
    $$D = \frac{E \cdot h^3}{12(1 - \nu^2)}$$
    Where $E$ is Young's modulus, $h$ is wall thickness, and $\nu$ is Poisson's ratio ($\nu \approx 0.33$). Crucially, rigidity scales linearly with material modulus ($E$), but scales with the cube of thickness ($h^3$).
  • The Magnesium Mass Advantage: Extruded 6061-T6 aluminum exhibits $E = 68.9\text{ GPa}$ with a density of $\rho = 2.70\text{ g/cm}^3$. Structural magnesium alloys (such as AZ91D and AM60B) have a lower modulus ($E = 45.0\text{ GPa}$), but a density of only $\rho = 1.81\text{ g/cm}^3$—fully 33% lighter than aluminum.
  • The Flexural Equivalence Calculation: Because magnesium is significantly less dense, an engineer can take the exact mass budget of a 0.60 mm aluminum wall and cast an equivalent-weight magnesium wall at $h = 0.895\text{ mm}$ (a $1.49\times$ thickness increase). Evaluating relative rigidity:
    $$\frac{D_{\text{Mg}}}{D_{\text{Al}}} = \left(\frac{E_{\text{Mg}}}{E_{\text{Al}}}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{h_{\text{Mg}}}{h_{\text{Al}}}\right)^3 = \left(\frac{45.0}{68.9}\right) \cdot (1.492)^3 \approx 0.653 \cdot 3.32 = 2.17$$
    At identical part weight, the panel's resistance to flexural deformation more than doubles (+117% increase in bending stiffness). Alternatively, magnesium can match baseline aluminum stiffness while cutting total enclosure mass by roughly 25%.
MANUFACTURING PROCESS PIPELINE // SEMI-SOLID INJECTION WORKFLOW CHIP FEEDSTOCK → UNIBODY ENCLOSURE
STEP 01: FEED
Argon Hopper Purge

Cold 1–4 mm AZ91D magnesium alloy chips gravity-feed into a sealed volumetric hopper purged with inert argon gas (O2 < 50 ppm) to prevent spontaneous melt combustion.

STEP 02: SHEAR
Slurry Rosette Milling

A reciprocating screw inside a 3-zone bimetallic barrel (350°C → 520°C → 575°C) shears dendritic crystal arms as they freeze, producing spherical α-Mg rosettes in eutectic liquid ($f_s \approx 0.12 - 0.18$).

STEP 03: INJECT
High-Speed Hydraulic Surge

Nitrogen accumulators surge the screw forward at 5.5 m/s with 120 MPa (1,200 bar) pressure, driving a cohesive laminar wave across the 0.50 mm cavity in 14–18 milliseconds.

STEP 04: SOLIDIFY
Conformal Die Chilling

Dievar tool steel molds with 210°C synthetic oil channels prevent premature freezing. Thin-wall parts cool with <1.5% volumetric shrinkage and <0.2% gas porosity.

STEP 05: PASSIVATE
CNC Trim & MAO Armor

A 90-second secondary CNC cleanup finishes hinge threads and cosmetic chamfers, followed by Micro-Arc Oxidation (MAO) growing a 12 μm ceramic MgAl2O4 spinel barrier.

PROCESS ARCHITECTURE: The 5-stage automated thixomolding sequence transforming chipped magnesium granules directly into ultra-thin near-net-shape structural laptop enclosures in an 18-second cycle. FLOWCHART 01

Historically, mechanical designers avoided magnesium because standard high-pressure die casting (HPDC) could not reliably produce cosmetic walls below 1.0 mm without severe internal porosity, high scrap rates, and melt fire risks. The breakthrough that solved this contradiction is Semi-Solid Thixomolding.

2. The Slurpee State: Why Semi-Solid Metal Flows Like Soft-Serve

Unlike pure metals that freeze at a discrete temperature, light alloys solidify over a broad thermal band bounded by the solidus and liquidus temperatures. For electronics-grade AZ91D (9.0% Al, 0.7% Zn, 0.2% Mn, balance Mg), the solidus is 470°C and the liquidus is 595°C, creating an immense 125°C semi-solid mushy freezing zone.

The Dendritic Solidification Trap: When molten magnesium cools undisturbed in a conventional die-casting sleeve, solid metal nucleates as branching, tree-like dendrites. As these dendritic arms interlock, they trap pockets of liquid eutectic. Solidification shrinkage in these trapped pockets creates microscopic voids and hot tears. Furthermore, this interlocking structure gives quiescent semi-solid metal the consistency of a rigid sponge, preventing it from filling sub-millimeter die features unless superheated past 640°C, which triggers violent turbulence and gas porosity.

The Physics of Thixotropic Shear-Thinning: Thixomolding avoids dendritic interlocking through rotational mechanical shear. Subjecting the alloy to continuous shear stress during solidification snaps fragile dendritic arms as soon as they nucleate. These fragments tumble in the shear field, ripening into smooth, spherical globular α-Mg rosettes (10–30 μm diameter) suspended in a liquid eutectic matrix.

This suspended slurry exhibits profound thixotropic shear-thinning rheology. At rest in the barrel, spherical rosettes lightly agglomerate, giving the semi-solid mass the high viscosity of heavy grease (~100 Pa·s). When the screw drives the slurry forward at high shear rates ($\dot{\gamma} > 10^4\text{ s}^{-1}$), inter-particle bonds release instantly. Dynamic viscosity collapses to 0.05 Pa·s—flowing almost as freely as water.

Laminar Cavity Filling Mechanics: The slurry acts as a Bingham pseudoplastic. When injected at 2.0 to 5.5 m/s, it does not atomize into a turbulent spray like liquid metal in die casting ($\text{Re} > 15{,}000$). Instead, high viscosity along tool boundaries stabilizes the flow front, driving a cohesive laminar frontal wave ($\text{Re} < 2{,}100$).

As this wave advances across a 0.50 mm cavity, it pushes cavity air ahead like a squeegee, venting through perimeter chill channels without entraining micro-bubbles. This laminar filling eliminates gas entrainment porosity, reducing internal gas voids from the 3.5% typical of die casting down to <0.2%. Because parts are pore-free, thixomolded components can undergo T6 heat treatment or high-temperature paint baking without blistering.

FIG 02 — HIGH-RESOLUTION RECIPROCATING SCREW THIXOMOLDING BARREL ARCHITECTURE SOLID FRACTION: f_s = 0.12 • INJECTION VELOCITY: 5.2 m/s
HIGH-RESOLUTION MACHINE SCHEMATIC: Vector cutaway of the Japan Steel Works (JSW) reciprocating screw thixomolding barrel, illustrating argon chip feeding, progressive shear-thinning thermal zones, and the 120 MPa hydraulic injection accumulator. FIGURE 02

3. Machine Architecture: The High-Speed Thermal Injection Barrel

Unlike cold-chamber die-casting machines that ladle molten metal from an external holding furnace into an open shot sleeve, a thixomolding press operates like a heavy-duty injection molding system adapted for metallurgy. Manufactured primarily by Japan Steel Works (JSW), these 450- to 1,200-ton presses integrate melting, shearing, metering, and injection into a sealed, automated cell.

The Argon-Shrouded Granular Feed: Magnesium reacts aggressively with atmospheric oxygen, igniting at 650°C into blinding white flames. Thixomolding completely eliminates open liquid pots and hazardous SF6 cover-gases. Instead, solid magnesium chips (1.0 to 4.0 mm granules) feed into a sealed volumetric hopper purged with inert argon gas (O2 maintained strictly below 50 ppm).

The Multi-Zone Bimetallic Barrel: Granules feed into a heavy-wall bimetallic barrel lined with high-strength Inconel 718 or Stellite. A reciprocating alloy screw rotates inside at 80–150 RPM, driven by a high-torque electric servo motor across three thermal zones:

  • Zone 1: Solid Feed (300°C to 400°C): Granules are compacted, degassed, and preheated by ceramic band heaters, forming a dynamic solid plug that seals against gas leakage.
  • Zone 2: Compression & Shear (500°C to 540°C): The screw's root diameter increases, forcing softening alloy into a narrowing channel. Above the 470°C solidus, primary crystals nucleate, but rotational shear between flight and barrel wall shears growing arms into spherical fragments.
  • Zone 3: Slurry Metering (565°C to 585°C): Induction coils tune the slurry to the target solid fraction ($f_s = 0.12$ to $0.18$). The screw pumps slurry forward through a check ring valve into the accumulation zone, pushing the screw backward to meter a precise 350-gram shot.

The High-Speed Hydraulic Shot Surge: Once metered, hydraulic nitrogen accumulators discharge into the injection piston. The screw surges forward at speeds up to 5.5 m/s with acceleration exceeding 40 Gs. Slurry drives through a heated nozzle into the die runner in less than 18 milliseconds, reaching an instantaneous intensification pressure of 120 MPa (1,200 bar) to pack out thin ribs before freezing.

FIG 03 — MICROSTRUCTURAL CROSS-SECTION: DIE-CAST VS. THIXOMOLDED VS. WROUGHT SEM ETCH: 2% NITAL • 500x MAGNIFICATION
METALLURGICAL GRAIN STRUCTURE: Scanning electron comparison illustrating why thixomolded magnesium achieves pore-free structural integrity compared to conventional die-casting gas cavities. FIGURE 03

4. Tool Steel Metallurgy & Thermal Fatigue (H13 vs. Uddeholm Dievar)

While thixomolding offers exceptional part properties, the core engineering challenge moves into mold tooling. Injecting semi-solid metal at 580°C under 120 MPa forces hardened steel die inserts to endure brutal cyclic thermal stress:

  • The Thermal Shock Cycle: Every 20 seconds, the cavity face heats violently from its resting preheat temperature of 200°C up to 580°C within 15 milliseconds as slurry enters. Internal cooling channels then extract sensible heat, chilling the face back to 200°C before mold opening. This generates severe cyclic compressive expansion during injection and tensile contraction during cooling.
  • The Failure of Standard AISI H13: Historically, toolmakers built molds from standard AISI H13 hot-work tool steel (vacuum hardened to 44–46 HRC). However, H13 contains relatively high silicon (~1.0% Si). Silicon promotes the segregation of brittle intermetallic phases along grain boundaries, lowering fracture toughness. Under the rapid thermal cycling of thixomolding, standard H13 suffers from catastrophic heat checking (network micro-cracking) after only 60,000 to 80,000 shots.
  • The Superiority of Uddeholm Dievar: To achieve production tool lives exceeding 250,000 to 350,000 shots without surface crazing, premier tooling shops mandate premium modified Cr-Mo-V tool steels, specifically Uddeholm Dievar or Böhler W403 VMR. Dievar drastically reduces silicon to 0.20% while boosting molybdenum to 2.30%. This chemical modification yields exceptional temper resistance and nearly doubles room-temperature Charpy V-notch impact toughness (>18 Joules versus 8–10 Joules for H13). Dievar's immense resistance to crack initiation allows toolmakers to hold razor-sharp 0.30 mm cosmetic shut-off lands across hundreds of thousands of production cycles.
  • Pressurized Conformal Hot-Oil Cooling: Unlike plastic molding tools that circulate cold water, thixomolding dies must never run cold. Cold water causes slurry to freeze immediately upon touching the gate, resulting in short-shots. Thixomolding molds integrate high-temperature conformal cooling channels circulating synthetic heat-transfer oil maintained at 180°C to 220°C under 6 bar pressure, keeping cavity walls hot to pack out 0.50 mm ribs before freezing.

5. DFM Guidelines for Ultra-Thin Unibodies: Ribbing, Radii, and Weld Lines

Designing a thixomolded unibody requires adhering to strict semi-solid fluid mechanics:

  1. Nominal Wall Thickness Bounds: The target cosmetic wall thickness for unibody laptops should be set between 0.50 mm and 0.65 mm. While localized flow paths can achieve 0.40 mm over short travel distances (<40 mm), attempting to push 0.40 mm across a 320 mm 14-inch laptop top-case causes excessive pressure drops ($\Delta P \propto \frac{1}{h^3}$), forcing the machine to run at extreme intensification pressures that cause parting-line flash.
  2. Wall Thickness Transition Slope Ratios: When transitioning from a thick functional zone (such as a 1.2 mm hinge boss) down to a 0.55 mm nominal cosmetic skin, never use abrupt 90-degree steps. Abrupt steps disrupt the laminar flow front, triggering localized flow separation, air traps, and sink marks. Always incorporate gradual transitional tapers with a minimum 3:1 ramp slope ratio (length to step height).
  3. Structural Stiffening Rib Geometry: To prevent sink marks on the outer A-surface of the enclosure, the base thickness of internal stiffening ribs should never exceed 0.45x to 0.55x the nominal wall thickness (e.g. a 0.28 mm rib on a 0.55 mm skin). Ribs must incorporate a minimum draft angle of 1.5° to 2.0° per side and a generous root fillet radius of $R \ge 0.25\text{ mm}$ to minimize notch stress concentration during drop impacts.
  4. Draft Angles and Thermal Shrinkage Clamping: Magnesium exhibits high volumetric thermal shrinkage during cooling (0.60% to 0.75% linear shrinkage). As the enclosure solidifies in the mold cavity, it contracts tightly around male internal core pins. Internal boss features and vertical ribbing require a strict minimum draft angle of 1.5°, while outer cosmetic perimeter walls can run as tight as 0.75° to 1.0°. Ejector pins must be positioned generously directly beneath rib intersections, designed with large surface areas to prevent punching holes through warm 0.55 mm walls during ejection.
  5. Weld Line Positioning: When slurry flows around internal cutouts (such as keyboard apertures or trackpad windows), the divided flow streams reunite on the downstream side to form a weld line (knit line). In semi-solid metals, if the two uniting flow fronts have cooled below 560°C, the solid rosettes fail to fuse across the interface, creating a mechanical notch that reduces tensile strength by up to 45%. Tool designers use sequential valve gates (SVGs) and vacuum chill overflows to draw cold metal beyond the cosmetic boundary, ensuring weld lines fuse at full temperature under active hydraulic pressure.

6. Unit Economics & Breakeven Modeling: Thixomolding vs. 5-Axis CNC Hogging

Evaluating enclosure manufacturing involves balancing high recurring piece costs against upfront tooling capital.

The Anatomy of CNC Billet Hogging: A 14-inch aluminum laptop unibody begins as an extruded 6061-T6 aluminum billet (330 x 230 x 18 mm) weighing 1,450 grams. Across three 5-axis CNC setups, carbide endmills mill internal cavities, keyboard wells, and battery bays down to a finished mass of just 135 grams. Over 90% of the metal is converted into scrap chips (buy-to-fly ratio of 10.7:1), requiring 42 to 55 minutes of spindle time per part and large CNC machine fleets.

The Near-Net-Shape Thixomolding Math: Thixomolding produces near-net-shape parts in an 18-second cycle time from an initial 165-gram shot. After robotic extraction, a trim die removes runners in 2 seconds, and excess runners are ground back into granules for closed-loop hopper reuse. A secondary CNC fixture performs light finishing—milling hinge threads, cosmetic chamfers, and antenna apertures—in just 90 seconds of spindle time instead of 45 minutes.

The Economic Breakeven Curve: At production volumes below 4,500 units, CNC machining is economically superior because there is virtually zero hard tooling capital expenditure ($12,000 for vacuum jigs versus $145,000 for a Dievar tool mold). However, as production scales past the 6,000-unit breakeven crossover, the astronomical cycle time and material waste of CNC hogging penalize the project. At 250,000 units (a typical flagship consumer laptop production run), thixomolding saves over $7.5 million in unit production costs while consuming 80% less factory floor space and embodied electricity.

7. Ceramic Armor: Micro-Arc Oxidation vs. Anodizing

Magnesium is the most electrochemically active engineering metal, with a standard reduction potential of $E^\circ = -2.37\text{ V}$ (-1.66 V for aluminum). In contact with noble metals (steel fasteners, brass inserts, copper pipes) in humid, saline conditions (palm sweat), bare magnesium acts as a sacrificial anode, corroding rapidly into white $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ powder.

Why Magnesium Cannot Be Anodized Like Aluminum: Acidic anodizing vigorously dissolves magnesium while releasing hydrogen gas. In alkaline conditions, it forms magnesium hydroxide, but $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ has a porous Pilling-Bedworth ratio (<1.0) that spalls off in acidic atmospheric moisture.

The Micro-Arc Oxidation (MAO / PEO) Revolution: To solve magnesium's corrosion vulnerability, modern consumer electronics manufacturers utilize Micro-Arc Oxidation (MAO), also known as Plasma Electrolytic Oxidation (PEO).

  • The Plasma Micro-Discharge Mechanism: The thixomolded enclosure is submerged in an environmentally friendly alkaline electrolyte bath containing sodium silicate, potassium hydroxide, and sodium aluminate. An immense bipolar pulsed AC electric potential (380 V to 550 V at frequencies between 100 Hz and 2 kHz) is applied across the bath.
  • Substrate Surface Fusion: Once the voltage exceeds the dielectric breakdown threshold of the growing surface oxide film, thousands of microscopic plasma micro-arcs erupt continuously across the magnesium surface. Localized temperatures inside these micro-discharge channels exceed 2,500°C with localized pressures surpassing 100 atmospheres.
  • Crystalline Spinel Ceramic Conversion: This extreme plasma energy locally melts the substrate magnesium and fuses it with aluminate and silicate ions from the electrolyte, synthesizing an ultra-dense, crystalline magnesium aluminate spinel ($ ext{MgAl}_2 ext{O}_4$) and alpha-alumina ceramic phase directly out of the base metal.
  • Environmental Robustness: Unlike standard chromate conversion coatings that offer weak mechanical durability, a 12-micron MAO ceramic layer is metallurgically grown from the metal itself—it cannot peel or delaminate. In standardized ASTM B117 neutral salt spray testing, MAO-treated magnesium enclosures survive over 500 continuous hours of 5% sodium chloride fog with zero pitting corrosion. Furthermore, the micro-porous outer ceramic crust provides an exceptional mechanical keying anchor for automated robotic electrostatic polyurethane (PU) soft-touch spray coatings, matching the cosmetic hand-feel of luxury ceramics.

8. Mechanical Impact & Drop Metrology: Energy Absorption and Internal Damping

In portable hardware, the ultimate structural test is the MIL-STD-810H corner drop test: dropping a 1.2 kg laptop from 1.2 meters (4 feet) onto solid steel plate at a 45-degree angle.

The Physics of Impact Deceleration: The 14.1 Joules of kinetic energy must dissipate within 2 to 4 milliseconds. Extruded 6061-T6 aluminum possesses high stiffness but low specific damping capacity (SDC = 4% to 8%). Because aluminum cannot absorb shock internally, acoustic stress waves (with sound speed $c = \sqrt{E / \rho} \approx 5{,}050\text{ m/s}$) reflect through the chassis, shattering display cover glass and cracking ceramic capacitors.

Magnesium's Atomic Damping Engine: Magnesium exhibits the highest specific damping capacity of any practical engineering metal—absorbing between 42% and 58% of dynamic vibration energy per cycle. The hexagonal close-packed (HCP) atomic crystal lattice of magnesium contains easily mobile dislocation segments that bow and unpin reversibly under cyclic mechanical shear, converting kinetic stress wave energy directly into harmless microscopic lattice heat via internal anelastic friction.

Alloy Selection for Drop Performance (AZ91D vs. AM60B): When configuring an enclosure assembly, mechanical engineers exploit two distinct magnesium alloys based on localized strain regimes:

  • AZ91D for Rigid Internal Mid-Plates: With 9.0% aluminum, AZ91D precipitates a high density of brittle intermetallic $\text{Mg}_{17}\text{Al}_{12}$ along its grain boundaries. This boosts tensile yield strength to 160 MPa with high hardness, making it the premier choice for internal chassis frames and keyboard deck stiffeners that must not bow under heavy typing loads.
